common_name: Singapore Pink Pickerelweed (Pink-Flowered Pickerel Weed Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2-6 inches deep at the pond margin in full sun once water has warmed after last frost.

directions: Singapore Pink is a named pink-flowered selection of pickerelweed, trading the species' usual blue-violet spikes for soft rosy-lavender blooms above the same glossy, arrow-shaped leaves. It tends to grow a bit more compactly than the straight species, making it a good fit for smaller water features and shallow tub gardens as well as open pond margins. Flowers open in succession from early summer through fall and draw bees and butterflies readily, so leave a few spent spikes in place if you want the plant to self-sow around the pond edge. Lift and divide crowded clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the planting vigorous and to share divisions.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Roy Davidson Yellow Flag Iris (Pale Yellow, Non-Seeding Water Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in wet, fertile soil in shallow standing water up to 6 inches deep or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Roy Davidson bears softer, pale creamy-yellow flowers with fine brown veining rather than the deep gold of the wild species, and each bloom holds open for about three days instead of the single day typical of straight yellow flag iris. It is prized among water gardeners because it rarely sets viable seed, giving the vigorous good looks and bold sword-shaped foliage of yellow flag without the aggressive self-sowing that has made the species invasive in many regions. Grow it at a pond margin or in a submerged container with standing water over the crown, in full sun for the best bloom. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or right after flowering to maintain vigor.

common_name: Berlin Tiger Yellow Flag Iris (Variegated Striped-Leaf, Veined-Flower Water Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in wet, fertile soil in shallow standing water up to 8-12 inches deep or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Berlin Tiger, raised by German iris breeder Tomas Tamberg, combines bright yellow flowers heavily veined in reddish-brown with bold, tiger-striped foliage marked in green, cream, and yellow, giving it year-round ornamental interest well beyond bloom time in late spring. The variegation is strongest on fresh spring growth and tends to green up somewhat as summer heat sets in, so site it where the early display will be most visible, such as at a pond margin or bog garden entrance. Like other yellow flag selections it tolerates shallow standing water over the crown and spreads gradually by rhizome, so give it room or plan to divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring. Confirm local invasive-species guidance before planting, since straight yellow flag iris is restricted in some regions even though named variegated forms are generally less commonly naturalized.

common_name: Rosea Plena Lotus (Double Rose-Pink Heirloom Lotus)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in a wide, undrained container submerged 6-12 inches deep in full sun once the water has warmed well past danger of frost.

directions: Rosea Plena is a historic Chinese lotus prized for its very full, deep rose-pink double flowers packed with dozens of petals that fade to a softer pink toward the edges, opening above large, umbrella-like blue-green leaves held well clear of the water. It is a vigorous, large-growing lotus, so give it a generous half-barrel, stock tank, or open pond bottom rather than a small tub, and feed with aquatic fertilizer tablets through the growing season for the biggest blooms. Like other hardy lotus it dies back completely to the tuber each winter and re-emerges in late spring once the water has warmed, so patience is needed before the first leaves appear. Divide overcrowded tubers every three to four years in spring, handling the brittle growing tips carefully since damage can prevent a division from sprouting.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society
